newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Journalists on pre-election attack over sleaze.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Journalists on pre-election attack over sleaze.

text.p: The day that former British trade minister Neil Hamilton abandoned his libel case against the Guardian, the newspaper alleged in a banner headline that he was "a liar and a cheat."
Now the reporters who pursued him on an influence-peddling trail have told all in a Perry Mason-style pageturner which paints a damning picture of Britain's ruling Conservative Party.
It pitches Hamilton and political lobbyist Ian Greer against the Guardian in a high-stakes poker game where each allegation of "sleaze" is answered with threats of legal action.
It could have ended in a sensational trial but instead was called off by the politician with just nine minutes to spare.
"They had taken it right to the precipice before blinking but in the end they blinked," journalists David Leigh and Ed Vulliamy write in "Sleaze: The Corruption of Parliament".

Hamilton quit as corporate affairs minister in October 1994, saying that he needed to fight to clear his name after allegations he accepted money and favours from Mohammed al-Fayed, the Egyptian-born owner of London's luxury Harrods store, in return for tabling questions in parliament.
GUARDIAN ALLEGATIONS
The Guardian alleged that Hamilton persistently asked for money from al-Fayed and would visit his office to collect cash payments.

Hamilton was also accused of failing to declare favours from al-Fayed, such as a six-night stay at the Paris Ritz when he is said to have enjoyed luxury meals with his wife and "laid siege" to the minibar in their room.
It is a breach of parliamentary rules to accept cash or favours in return for asking direct questions in the House of Commons.

Since the affair broke, members have agreed to tighten up rules on their links with lobbyists, effectively banning paid advocacy. They are also much stricter in declaring any money earned in connection with their jobs in parliament.

At the last moment, Hamilton and Greer abandoned what had been billed as the libel trial of the century. Angrily denying the Guardian's allegations, Hamilton said he was unable to afford the legal fees and claimed "They're doing a hatchet job on me."
Prime Minister John Major and his deputy Michael Heseltine had been subpoenaed to give evidence in what could have been an explosive court case.

When Hamilton withdrew, the Guardian went on the offensive on October 1, 1996, with claims that the case would have revealed "a pattern of parliamentary sleaze more far reaching than anyone had imagined".

It named four other senior Conservatives who it said were involved in a paid campaign to promote al-Fayed's interests. It based its claims on government documents released for the trial as well as witness statements.
SLEAZE FACTOR IN POLITICS

With an election due by May, the reporters have gone back into battle against the government which has lost nine ministers and seven senior members of parliament in a string of sexual and financial scandals since 1992.

The constant barrage of sleaze allegations prompted Major, widely recognised as one of the most honest men in British politics, to set up a special committee to look into standards of morality in public life.

Sleaze was even given an official definition by Lord Nolan, the judge heading the committee. He called it "a pervasive atmosphere...in which sexual, financial and governmental misconduct were indifferently linked."
The new book alleges that lobbyist Greer paid Hamilton to table parliamentary questions aimed at helping his clients.
The Guardian, reviewing the book after its recent release, compared it with the pursuit of former U.S president Richard Nixon by Washington Post reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein.
"There is a play in 'Sleaze' as well as a film which could be the British version of 'All the President's Men'," said reviewer Tom Paulin.

Author and critic Julian Barnes called the new book "a timely and dispiriting account of the Hamilton case." However, he said it lost some of its impact because the authors described virtually all Conservatives "in a tone of suppurating contempt."

But Barnes, reflecting the opinion poll perception that the deeply unpopular Conservatives have become stale, out-of-touch and arrogant after almost 18 years in power, said the 1990's logo of the ruling party could be "The Snout in the Minibar."
